podcast.title: Entry into Fleetwood Mac (1975)
podcast.body: She joined Fleetwood Mac in 1975, as her boyfriend Lindsey Buckingham made her inclusion a non-negotiable condition for his own acceptance into the band. "Lindsey Buckingham insisted that his girlfriend Stevie Nicks be accepted into what remained of Fleetwood Mac at that time when Lindsey Buckingham was invited to fill the void."

podcast.title: Music Video Endorsement (2001)
podcast.body: Stevie Nicks endorsed Destiny's Child's "pseudo cover" of her song "Edge of Seventeen" by appearing in the music video for their 2001 hit "Bootylicious," mirroring similar celebrity endorsements of reboots. "Stevie Nix endorsed this 2001 pseudo cover by appearing in Destiny's music video."

podcast.title: Abundance of Songs - Flowing Lacy Bell Sleeves
podcast.body: When Stevie Nicks joined Fleetwood Mac, she had an abundance of unreleased songs, humorously described as being "up her flowing lacy bell sleeves." This rich repertoire included "Landslide," which she contributed to the band's 1975 self-titled album. "Fortunately, Nix had more songs up her flowing lacy bell sleeves."

podcast.title: Affair and Relationship Splinter with Lindsey Buckingham
podcast.body: Though unmarried, Stevie Nicks and Lindsey Buckingham had been together for over half a decade, but their "fractious relationship" splintered permanently. This was attributed to Lindsey's controlling nature and an affair Stevie had during the making of "Rumours." "Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks, though unmarried, had been together for over half a decade, but their fractious relationship splintered permanently, done in by Lindsey's controlling nature and an affair Stevie had."

podcast.title: Aspiration for "Straight Up Rock and Roll"
podcast.body: Upon becoming a solo artist, Stevie Nicks expressed a desire to make a "Tom Petty album" and pursue "straight up rock and roll," indicating a preference for a harder sound than Fleetwood Mac's 70s "softer rock." "She wanted to make a Tom Petty album. At least that's what she said when she became a solo artist. She wanted to do what she called straight up rock and roll."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Cocaine Addiction and Rehab
podcast.body: During the recording of "Tango in the Night" in the mid-1980s, Stevie Nicks battled cocaine addiction and subsequently sought treatment at the Betty Ford Clinic. "especially Stevie Nicks, who actually went to rehab at the Betty Ford Clinic for her cocaine addiction."

podcast.title: Double Induction into Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
podcast.body: Stevie Nicks was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame twice: first with Fleetwood Mac in 1998, and then as a solo artist 21 years later, making her the first woman to achieve this honor. Twenty-two men had received this honor previously. "Stevie Nicks was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame for the second time. She was inducted with Fleetwood Mac in 1998, and then 21 years later as a solo artist."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Early Career Sexism Experience
podcast.body: Stevie Nicks recalled a single instance early in her career where a man in the crowd made "lute remarks," and legendary concert promoter Bill Graham immediately intervened, telling him to leave. She considered her overall experience with sexism in the industry to be relatively easy. "She can remember one time, very early in her career, when a guy in the crowd made some lute remarks to her, and the legendary concert promoter Bill Graham told him to essentially get the fuck out, and that was that."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Involvement in Internal Love Triangle
podcast.body: She was part of a "messy love triangle" with Lindsey Buckingham and Mick Fleetwood, a significant source of the intense internal drama and lyrical material for the band during the *Rumours* era. "relationship drama Stevie and Mick and Stevie and Lindsey form a messy love triangle."

podcast.title: Outsized Personality - Joining Fleetwood Mac
podcast.body: Stevie Nicks, along with Lindsey Buckingham, possessed an "outsized personality" that contributed to Fleetwood Mac's transformation into multi-platinum superstars when they joined in the mid-70s. This contrasted with Christine McVie's more self-effacing nature. "Vocalist Stevie Nicks, and guitarist and studio whiz Lindsey Buckingham."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Pledge with Christine McVie
podcast.body: On the day Stevie Nicks joined Fleetwood Mac, she and Christine McVie made a mutual vow never to be treated as "less than" or "second class citizens" within the male-dominated rock environment. They promised to fight for their place, ensure their songs and music were equally as good as the men's, and be included in creative discussions. "She said that they said to each other, we will never be treated like second class citizens. We will never be not allowed to hang out in a room full of intelligent, crazy rock and roll stars, because we are just as crazy and just as intelligent as they are."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Pre-Fleetwood Mac Performance - Fritz
podcast.body: Stevie Nicks had been performing with Lindsey Buckingham since the late 1960s, initially singing lead with his psychedelic rock band called Fritz. This early collaboration established their musical partnership before they formed Buckingham Nicks and later joined Fleetwood Mac. "Buckingham and Nix have been performing with each other since the late 60s when Lindsay got Stevie to sing lead with his psychedelic rock band Fritz."

podcast.title: Reveal of Christine McVie's Illness - Post-Mortem
podcast.body: A few days after Christine McVie's death on November 30, 2022, bandmate Stevie Nicks revealed that the rest of Fleetwood Mac hadn't known McVie was ill until immediately before her passing. This detail highlighted McVie's private nature, not wanting to trouble the world with her drama. "bandmate Stevie Nicks revealed that the rest of Fleetwood Mac hadn't even known McVee was ill until immediately before her death."

podcast.title: Romantic and Musical Partners - Buckingham Nicks Duo
podcast.body: Before joining Fleetwood Mac, Stevie Nicks and Lindsey Buckingham were both romantic and musical partners, performing together since the late 60s and releasing the album *Buckingham Nicks* in 1973. Their relationship dynamics would later become a significant part of Fleetwood Mac's drama. "Now a romantic couple as well as musical partners, the duo recorded Buckingham Nix with the cream of LA session players."

podcast.title: San Francisco Scene Influence
podcast.body: Stevie Nicks was part of the San Francisco music scene, learning from artists like Janis Joplin, Grace Slick, and Buffalo Springfield, which she considered a "literal rock and roll school." "Now, Stevie and Lindsey Buckingham were part of that whole San Francisco scene that Janice Joplin was part of. Stevie learned from watching Janice and Grace Slick and Buffalo Springfield, a literal rock and roll school."

xref.title: Tribute After Death
xref.body: Ozzy Osborne was among the many musicians who sent tributes upon Taylor Hawkins' death, underscoring the widespread respect and admiration he commanded from his peers. "When he died, tributes came in from everyone from Ozzy Osborne to Stevie Nicks, to Travis Barker, to Tom Morello to Liam Gallagher."

xref.title: Versatile Session Musician
xref.body: Beyond Motown, Bobby Jean Hall has an impressive client list that includes a diverse range of legendary artists. Her percussion work has graced albums by Bob Dylan, Lynyrd Skynyrd, Rod Stewart, Janis Joplin, Joni Mitchell, Dolly Parton, The Doobie Brothers, Aretha Franklin, Tracy Chapman, James Taylor, and Stevie Nicks, highlighting her status as a highly sought-after session player. "Other clients have included Bob Dylan, Leonard Skinner, Rod Stewart, Janice Joplin, Joni Mitchell, Dolly Parton, The Dooby Brothers, Aretha Franklin, Tracy Chapman, James Taylor, and Stevie Nicks."
